match.reason: The bank cards cover the mean only as one of several measures (mean, median, mode, range) or as part of choosing a centre with outliers, and neither teaches finding a missing value from a known mean, so the new point needs its own card.

draft.title: The mean
card: The mean is the total of the values divided by how many values there are. It is the average people often mean.
Example: Sam scores 6, 8, 7 and 11 in four quizzes. The total is \(6 + 8 + 7 + 11 = 32\). The mean is \(32 \div 4 = 8\).
If you know the mean, you can find the total. Total \(=\) mean \(\times\) number of values. In the example, \(8 \times 4 = 32\).

To find a missing value, work out the total needed, then take away the values you have. If the mean of 3 values is 10, the total is 30. Two values of 9 and 12 add to 21, so the third is \(30 - 21 = 9\).
draft.remember: Mean \(=\) total \(\div\) number of values. Mean \(\times\) number of values gives the total.

a.q: What is the mean of 4, 9, 5, 6 and 11?
a.why: The total is \(4 + 9 + 5 + 6 + 11 = 35\). There are 5 values, so the mean is \(35 \div 5 = 7\). The answer 35 is only the total: it has not been divided.
a.clue: Add the values, then divide by how many there are.

b.q: Priya's mean score in 4 maths tests is 15. Her scores in the first three tests are 12, 18 and 14. What was her score in the fourth test?
b.why: The total needed is \(15 \times 4 = 60\). The first three tests add to \(12 + 18 + 14 = 44\), so the fourth is \(60 - 44 = 16\). The answer 60 is the total of all four tests, not the missing score.
b.clue: Find the total of all four tests first.

check.summary: No problems found. The card's worked examples, both answers (7 and 16) and the explanations are all correct.
